summary: Gives instructions to IANA and the initial contents of the registries of assigned numbers used by the Secure Shell protocol. It is meant only for setting up the registries referenced by the set of SSH documents. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4250 records the initial numbers and names used by SSH and tells IANA how to manage future additions. It is a registry document, not a definition of a new SSH protocol.

questions: what are the ssh assigned numbers
what is the ssh private use range
subtitle: The initial registries and assignment rules for numbers and names used by the SSH protocol.

tldr.problem: SSH protocol documents need shared number and name assignments for messages, errors, terminal modes, and algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4250 initializes the IANA registries and specifies how future assignments are reviewed, including ranges reserved for private use.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new SSH protocol and has been updated by RFC 8268, RFC 9142 and RFC 9519.

today: RFC 4250 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8268, RFC 9142 and RFC 9519. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Allocation Rules
sections.content:
This document initializes the IANA registries referenced by the SSH architecture, transport, authentication, and connection documents. It also sets rules for future assignments. Except for identifying one Historic algorithm, it does not define a new protocol or number range.

Registry terms such as PRIVATE USE, IETF CONSENSUS, and STANDARDS ACTION have allocation meanings defined by the referenced registry guidance. The document also establishes a convention for showing SSH field names and example values.
sections.plainLanguage: This document lists the starting contents of SSH registries. It also explains how new numbers and names are approved.

sections.title: SSH Message Number Ranges
sections.content:
Every SSH packet begins with a one-byte message number, from 1 to 255. The ranges group messages by protocol layer: transport, algorithm negotiation, key exchange, user authentication, connection management, and channel operations. Numbers 128 to 191 are reserved for client protocols; 192 to 255 are for local extensions.

New assignments use different review rules depending on the range. Some require a Standards Action, while the client-protocol range uses IETF Consensus. IANA does not control the local-extension range.
sections.plainLanguage: An SSH message number identifies the kind of message that follows. The number's range also identifies the SSH function it belongs to.

sections.title: Disconnection and Channel Error Codes
sections.content:
The registries include 32-bit disconnection reasons and channel-open failure reasons. Initial disconnection values include host not allowed, protocol error, and connection lost. Initial channel failure values include administrative prohibition, connection failure, unknown channel type, and resource shortage.

Future values are assigned sequentially through IETF Consensus. A range beginning at 0xFE000000 is left for private use. For channel failure codes, the RFC describes a subrange for locally assigned channel types and a separate range intended for experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: SSH uses reason codes to identify why a connection or channel could not continue. Some values are assigned through the standards process, and others are reserved for local use.

sections.title: Encoded Terminal Modes
sections.content:
A pseudo-terminal request includes a byte stream of terminal-mode opcodes and arguments. Opcodes are one byte each. Opcodes from 1 to 159 have a 32-bit argument; opcodes from 160 to 255 were not defined by this document.

The initial assignments include terminal controls such as VINTR, ECHO, and CS8, plus input and output speed settings. New opcodes require IETF Consensus. The RFC notes that not every terminal mode is supported by every system.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudo-terminal request can carry numbered settings for the remote terminal. Each setting tells the receiving system how the terminal should behave.

sections.title: Names and Algorithm Registries
sections.content:
Registered SSH names use printable US-ASCII, are case-sensitive, and must not contain certain characters or exceed 64 characters. Names containing an at-sign are local extensions and are not registered or controlled by IANA; the domain portion must be a fully qualified domain name controlled by the name's author.

The initial registries include service names, authentication methods, channel types, requests, key-exchange methods, and encryption, message-authentication, public-key, and compression algorithms. This RFC assigns the names; the SSH protocol documents describe the algorithms themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: SSH uses names as well as numbers for protocol options. Registered names follow shared rules, while names with a domain suffix can be defined locally.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says SSH provides a secure encrypted channel over an insecure network. It does not add security mechanisms beyond the registry assignments.

The full security considerations for SSH are in the SSH architecture document, RFC 4251. The names and values listed here identify protocol options but do not define their security behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lists identifiers, not the security design of SSH. The SSH architecture document contains the broader security considerations.
